newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Interest groups worry Australia Wallis member.
newsitem.headline: Interest groups worry Australia Wallis member.

text.p: A member of the Wallis inquiry into the Australian financial system said on Monday he was concerned the report's recommendations would not be enacted due to pressure from political parties and other interest groups.
"We hope not to die a death of a thousand cuts," investment banker Bill Beerworth told a banking conference.

"The government is going to announce in a couple of months what it proposes to do," Beerworth said. "Of course the forces of darkness are out there trying to knock off this recommendation, that change, and so on...," he said.

He also said described the government's prerequisite that mergers among the big four banks would not be sanctioned until there had been a marked improvement in small business lending as an almost "unfulfillable condition".

The Wallis inquiry report, which was released by the government on April 9, recommended the end of the so-called "six pillars" policy which prevented mergers between the four major banks in Australia and the two largest local insurance groups.
In its response, the goverment ended the policy but said the big four banks could not merge until the market for small business had improved with more competition and cheaper rates.

Beerworth said margins on small business loans should be higher than other commercial loans due to the risky and unpredictable nature of the sector. "It is inevitable that rates for small business ought to be higher than for vanilla lending."

The government has not set a benchmark for what it regarded as an improvement in the market for small business lending, he said. "I would imagine that the banks will be talking to the government about precisely what it means, what the outcomes are that the government is looking for," he later told Reuters.
The big four banks are National Australia Bank Ltd, Commonwealth Bank of Australia, Westpac Banking Corp and Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd.
The latter two had been regarded as prime takeover targets before the government's response to the Wallis report was known, with National Australia seen as the most likely predator.
Australia's two largest insurance companies are the Australian Mutual Provident Society (AMP) and the French-controlled National Mutual Holdings Ltd.
AMP said on the weekend it would probably seek a banking licence in the near future and has said it would not contemplate a takeover of one of the bank majors.
